hazards.blocked-exit-gurney: That gurney is parked across the fire exit while you finish up. An egress path blocked even for a few minutes is a hazard for everyone on this floor, not just an inconvenience for whoever needs it next.
hazards.expired-o2-tag: That transport oxygen tank's inspection tag is expired. A tank that hasn't been checked on schedule is not the one you grab for a patient who needs oxygen during the trip — pull a current one instead.
hazards.solo-lift-attempt: That's a one-person lift on a patient who needs a gait belt and a second set of hands. Safe patient handling exists because a solo manual lift is exactly the motion that puts a career-ending back injury on the transport tech and the patient both — not because it's slower to ask for help.
hazards.unlocked-brake-decoy: That wheelchair is standing on a ramp with its brakes off. An unlocked chair on any grade rolls the moment weight shifts onto it — brakes get set before anyone reaches for the seat, every time, ramp or flat floor.

interrupts.alert: Right after standing, the patient says they feel dizzy and unsteady.
interrupts.cue: That gets reported before this trip continues, not noted for later.
interrupts.missNote: The trip continued with an unreported dizzy spell on the record nowhere. Whatever caused it is now travelling with the patient instead of being looked at where it happened.
interrupts.why: Dizziness right after a position change is exactly the kind of thing a transport tech isn't the one to judge — it gets escalated to the nursing staff immediately, because continuing the trip on a guess about whether it's nothing is not a call this job makes alone.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the call to the nurse — a patient reporting dizziness gets looked at before the trip goes anywhere else.

interrupts.alert: Partway across the slide board, the receiving bed rolls slightly — its brake was never set.
interrupts.cue: The slide stops until the bed is actually secured.
interrupts.missNote: The transfer finished across a bed that was never actually secured. The gap between the board and a bed that can still move is exactly where a patient ends up on the floor instead of on the mattress.
interrupts.why: A slide-board transfer only works because both surfaces it bridges are fixed — a bed that can roll turns a controlled slide into an uncontrolled one, and it gets locked down before the transfer continues, not finished quickly to get past the wobble.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the bed's brake — lock it down before the slide continues.

lateNotes.log-complete: Hold that. The equipment goes back to its dock before this trip logs as finished.
lateNotes.verbal-handoff: There's no one to report to yet — get this patient off the elevator and to the unit first.

name: Patient Transport & Safe Handling

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Read the patient's ID band and match it to the name and destination on the ticket.
steps.prompt: Read the patient's ID band and match it to the name and destination on the ticket.
steps.title: Verify the ID band against the transport ticket
steps.why: A transport ticket sends the right equipment to the right room, but only the ID band on the patient's own wrist confirms this is actually the person that ticket is for — moving the wrong patient is a mistake this one check exists to catch before it starts.

steps.cue: Set both wheel brakes on the wheelchair before the patient stands.
steps.prompt: Set both wheel brakes on the wheelchair before the patient stands.
steps.title: Lock the brakes before the transfer
steps.why: A wheelchair that rolls even a few centimeters while someone is mid-stand is how a controlled transfer becomes a fall — the brakes get checked and locked before anyone puts weight on the footrests or the seat.

steps.cue: Read the tank gauge and confirm it's in the safe range for the trip before switching over.

gauge.label: TANK PRESSURE
gauge.missNote: Committed on a reading that wasn't actually in range. Switch to a tank you've confirmed before this patient leaves the room.

steps.prompt: Read the tank gauge and confirm it's in the safe range for the trip before switching over.
steps.title: Check the transport oxygen tank before disconnecting wall O2
steps.why: A transport tank has to carry enough for the trip plus a margin, per its own gauge — switching over on a tank you haven't actually read is how a patient on oxygen ends up between floors with none.

steps.cue: Apply the gait belt, stand and pivot together, then seat the patient in the wheelchair.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Belt on first, then the stand-and-pivot, then seated — skipping straight to the pivot leaves nothing secure to control the movement with.
steps.prompt: Apply the gait belt, stand and pivot together, then seat the patient in the wheelchair.
steps.robotNote: A gait-belt transfer is hands-on a person's body; this one stays with the transport crew.
steps.title: Transfer with a gait belt, not a solo lift
steps.why: The gait belt gives the transport tech a secure hold on the patient's center of gravity instead of an arm or a gown — paired with a second set of hands, it's what turns a stand-and-pivot into a controlled movement instead of a lift either person is doing alone.

steps.cue: Check the chart's fall-risk flag and clip on the matching yellow band before the trip starts.
steps.prompt: Check the chart's fall-risk flag and clip on the matching yellow band before the trip starts.
steps.title: Apply the fall-risk indicator already on the chart
steps.why: The flag is already on the chart — this step is carrying it through, not deciding it. Every unit this patient passes through reads that band on sight, which is the whole point of it following the patient rather than staying on a door nobody's near anymore.

steps.cue: Two things in this room will cause a problem the second this chair starts moving. Find them.

itemNames.loose-iv-line: an IV line that will snag on the doorway
itemNames.untucked-footrest: a footrest not folded up for the transfer

itemNotes.loose-iv-line: That line is hanging loose enough to catch on the doorframe the moment this chair moves — it gets gathered and clipped to the pole before you push off, not sorted out after it's already pulled taut.
itemNotes.untucked-footrest: A footrest left down at knee height is exactly what a patient's shin catches on standing up or sitting down — fold it clear before the transfer, not after someone's already bumped it.

steps.prompt: Two things in this room will cause a problem the second this chair starts moving. Find them.
steps.title: Scan the room before you move
steps.why: A trip that starts smoothly and snags on the doorway thirty seconds later is not a trip that started safely — the room gets checked for exactly this kind of thing before the wheels ever turn, not fixed on the fly once something's already caught.

steps.cue: Swing the footrests back into position and confirm they're locked.
steps.prompt: Swing the footrests back into position and confirm they're locked.
steps.title: Deploy the footrests for the ride
steps.why: Footrests folded up for the transfer go back down and lock before the chair moves anywhere — a foot dragging along the floor the whole trip is its own injury, separate from the one the transfer itself was built to avoid.

steps.cue: Press and hold the door-open control while the chair rolls fully inside.
steps.holdBreakNote: You let go before the chair was fully clear of the doors. A door that closes on a wheelchair, a pole or a limb doesn't ask whether you meant to release the button.
steps.prompt: Press and hold the door-open control while the chair rolls fully inside.
steps.title: Hold the elevator door while boarding
steps.why: A standard elevator door's timer is built for someone walking through empty-handed, not a wheelchair, an IV pole and a tech backing it in — holding the door open is what keeps it from closing on the equipment or the patient mid-load.

steps.cue: Load the wheelchair so the patient faces the doors, per the building's own transport convention.
steps.prompt: Load the wheelchair so the patient faces the doors, per the building's own transport convention.
steps.title: Position the equipment foot-end first
steps.why: This building's transport routing is written the same way for every crew so nobody has to work out chair orientation fresh on every ride — following it here is what keeps the patient facing out, clear of the closing doors, and the tech in control of the chair the whole ride.

steps.cue: Give the receiving staff a verbal report, then update the tracking log with the patient's new location.
steps.outOfOrderNote: The verbal report comes first, while the receiving staff is standing right here — the log update is what makes that report findable later, not a replacement for saying it out loud.
steps.prompt: Give the receiving staff a verbal report, then update the tracking log with the patient's new location.
steps.title: Hand off to the receiving unit
steps.why: A ticket dropped at a desk tells nobody anything until someone happens to read it — a verbal handoff means the receiving unit knows this patient arrived the moment they actually did, and the tracking log is what lets the next person who needs to find this patient actually do it.

steps.cue: Set the brakes before this patient transfers out of the chair.
steps.prompt: Set the brakes before this patient transfers out of the chair.
steps.title: Lock the brakes again at the destination
steps.why: The brakes get set fresh at every stop this trip makes — the ones locked back at the first room mean nothing to a chair that's been rolled, turned and ridden in an elevator since then.

steps.cue: Bridge the board between the chair and the bed and hold a steady, controlled slide.
steps.holdBreakNote: The slide broke off partway across the board. A patient left mid-slide on an unsupported board is worse off than one who never started moving.
steps.prompt: Bridge the board between the chair and the bed and hold a steady, controlled slide.
steps.title: Slide-board the patient to the bed
steps.why: A slide board lets the patient's weight move across a smooth bridge instead of being lifted by hand — holding the slide steady rather than rushing it is what keeps the board from shifting out from under the patient halfway across.

steps.cue: Wheel the chair back to its charging dock and plug it in.
steps.prompt: Wheel the chair back to its charging dock and plug it in.
steps.title: Return the equipment to its dock
steps.why: Equipment left wherever the last trip ended is equipment the next trip can't find charged and ready — docking it now is what makes the next tech's trip start on time instead of hunting the floor for a working chair.

steps.cue: Close out the transport ticket in the system.
steps.prompt: Close out the transport ticket in the system.
steps.title: Log the trip complete
steps.why: An open ticket reads as a patient still in transit — closing it the moment the trip actually ends is what keeps the tracking board honest for whoever's watching it for the next request.

supportLine: your employer's employee assistance program, or SEIU-UHW's member resources if a close call on a transfer has you shaken
tagline: ID checked against the ticket, brakes locked before every transfer, a gait belt instead of a solo lift, the route scanned for a line or a footrest that bites, and a real handoff at the other end
